\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.

\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.

All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
Our Ordinal Boundary Detection (OBD) head leverages this ordered structure, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.

\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.

The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.

\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Boundary Detection (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.

Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.

\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
Early statistical approaches such as GLTR~\cite{gehrmann2019gltr} visualized per-token likelihood ranks to help human annotators spot generated text, establishing that token-level distributional cues are informative for detection.
Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
Hans et al.~\cite{hans2024binoculars} proposed Binoculars, which computes the cross-perplexity ratio between two closely related language models to achieve near-perfect detection without any training data.
DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.

All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Boundary Detection (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.

\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.

\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
D4~\cite{tirumala2023d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2023doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.

The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.

\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

# Abstract v2

## Abstract

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by recursive synthetic content—text recursively generated across multiple generations. Information degrades monotonically per the Data Processing Inequality with each generation, yet no method estimates a document's generational depth. We introduce the first systematic framework for generational depth estimation, combining a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth. We empirically measure the discrimination boundary K*, defined as the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain statistically distinguishable. Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total) at the ≤1.5B parameter scale, we find K*=2 is consistent: for the four model-mode configurations, bootstrap 95% CI lower bounds for 1-vs-2 all exceed θ=0.60 while all 2-vs-3 CI upper bounds fall below it; the four decoding strategies likewise yield point-estimate AUC above θ at 1-vs-2 and below at 2-vs-3. Cross-model transfer shows classifiers retain 80–92% accuracy across generators, with binary (0-vs-1) AUC exceeding 0.96, indicating depth features are largely text-intrinsic. Preliminary neural probing on one dataset yields K*_neural=3, suggesting our 15-feature K*=2 is a representation-dependent lower bound. Frontier LLMs achieve ~88% binary detection but only ~33% five-class depth accuracy—below our OBD classifier's 38.6%—confirming depth estimation as a non-trivial task requiring specialized features. Our findings motivate a three-tier taxonomy (human / generation-1 / generation-2+) for depth-aware data curation; we investigate whether this coarse ordinal signal enables graduated filtering that outperforms binary approaches discarding all synthetic content indiscriminately.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
\label{sec:discuss_kstar}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ uniformly across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations from Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary} and 4 decoding strategies from the ablation)---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.

The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.

The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.

This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6114, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discriminable depth horizon extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow regardless of feature expressiveness.
These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.

The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$, with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.

\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:discuss_transfer}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs.
At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across generators.

The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.

Two caveats bound this conclusion.
First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:discuss_features}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.

This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.

The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}

Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11).
Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).

This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.

\emph{Model scale.}
All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.

\emph{Language and domain.}
All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
Sensitivity analysis across four decoding configurations shows $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 2$ for $\theta \in [0.60, 0.65]$, and $\Kempirical = 1$ at $\theta = 0.70$ (3 of 4 configurations).
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

# Abstract v2

## Abstract

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by recursive synthetic content—text recursively generated across multiple generations. Information degrades monotonically per the Data Processing Inequality with each generation, yet no method estimates a document's generational depth. We introduce the first systematic framework for generational depth estimation, combining a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth. We empirically measure the discrimination boundary K*, defined as the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain statistically distinguishable. Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total) at the ≤1.5B parameter scale, we find K*=2 is consistent: for the four model-mode configurations, bootstrap 95% CI lower bounds for 1-vs-2 all exceed θ=0.60 while all 2-vs-3 CI upper bounds fall below it; the four decoding strategies likewise yield point-estimate AUC above θ at 1-vs-2 and below at 2-vs-3. Cross-model transfer shows classifiers retain 80–92% accuracy across generators, with binary (0-vs-1) AUC exceeding 0.96, indicating depth features are largely text-intrinsic. Preliminary neural probing on one dataset yields K*_neural=3, suggesting our 15-feature K*=2 is a representation-dependent lower bound. Frontier LLMs achieve ~88% binary detection but only ~33% five-class depth accuracy—below our OBD classifier's 38.6%—confirming depth estimation as a non-trivial task requiring specialized features. Our findings motivate a three-tier taxonomy (human / generation-1 / generation-2+) for depth-aware data curation; we investigate whether this coarse ordinal signal enables graduated filtering that outperforms binary approaches discarding all synthetic content indiscriminately.

% === Contribution 1: K*=2 universal boundary ===
% Sources: exp_007 (bootstrap CI + permutation), exp_001/exp_002/exp_017/mvp_pilot (model-mode), exp_003 (decoding ablation)
We presented the first systematic measurement of the generational depth
discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
Across three model architectures in four model-mode configurations
(Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode; Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both
continuation and rewrite modes) and 4 decoding strategies---totaling 8
conditions---we establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a universal boundary:
classifiers reliably distinguish adjacent generations up to depth~2, but all
deeper pairs fall below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$.
For the four model-mode configurations, bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
and permutation tests confirm statistical significance at the 1v2 boundary
($p \leq 0.002$ for all four); the most marginal case, Qwen-continuation,
yields a CI lower bound of 0.6015, exceeding $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp.
All four decoding configurations (greedy, nucleus, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$)
likewise yield 1v2 point-estimate $\auc$ above $\theta$.
The 0v1 boundary is near-perfectly separable ($\auc > 0.99$), followed by a
sharp ${\sim}$30\,pp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$: 0.6112--0.7039 across all
conditions), while all 2v3 pairs fall below~$\theta$.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose discriminable
statistical fingerprint is exhausted within two steps.

% === Contribution 2: Ordinal depth estimation framework ===
% Sources: exp_010 (OBD vs baselines), exp_013 (cross-model transfer), exp_005 (feature degradation), exp_011 (LLM zero-shot)

decomposition (OBD) framework pairing 15 hand-crafted statistical features
with LightGBM classifiers.
Cross-model transfer experiments demonstrate 80--92\% accuracy retention
across continuation-mode model pairs, with
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieving 90--92\% and 0v1 transfer $\auc$
exceeding 0.96 universally---indicating that depth signals are largely
text-intrinsic rather than generator-specific.
Feature degradation orderings are consistent across architectures
(Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features dominating
uniformly, suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the
autoregressive mechanism itself.
As a reference point, frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus~4.6) achieve
${\sim}$88\% binary human-vs.-synthetic accuracy but only ${\sim}$33\% on
5-class depth estimation, below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\%---confirming that
fine-grained depth discrimination requires specialized statistical features
rather than general language understanding.
A preliminary neural probing experiment suggests that this operational bound is not tight: a frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder paired with an MLP classifier achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ versus 0.5609 with hand-crafted features), indicating that learned representations recover depth signal beyond the 15-dimensional feature set.

Our findings are bounded by the scale of models tested ($\leq$1.5B parameters), restriction to English C4 text, and the use of prompt-chain rather than retrain-chain protocols; the 15-dimensional feature set yields $\Kempirical$ as an operational lower bound, and $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
\label{sec:discuss_kstar}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ uniformly across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations from Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary} and 4 decoding strategies from the ablation)---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.

The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.

The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.

This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

Importantly, $\Kempirical = 2$ is an \emph{operational} lower bound conditioned on the 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set; the \emph{theoretical} boundary $\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher.
Preliminary evidence from a neural probing experiment supports this distinction.
A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B encoder (1536-dimensional last-layer representations) paired with a lightweight MLP classifier achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$ ($\text{std} = 0.0094$) on the Qwen-continuation dataset, exceeding the $\theta = 0.60$ threshold that the same dataset's LightGBM classifier fails to cross ($\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$: the learned representation recovers one additional discriminable boundary that the hand-crafted features miss.
The improvement is concentrated at the 2v3 pair ($+$5.86\,pp over LightGBM); at the already-separable 1v2 boundary the neural probe achieves 0.6983 versus 0.6114, a substantial gain but one that does not alter the boundary determination.
At 3v4, the neural probe reaches $\auc = 0.5930$---below $\theta$ but closer to the threshold than any hand-crafted configuration---suggesting that a still richer representation might push the boundary further.
The lossy-channel narrative remains intact: even with 1536-dimensional frozen representations, the discriminable depth horizon extends to only three steps, confirming that the information bottleneck of recursive generation is shallow regardless of feature expressiveness.
These results are preliminary: they cover a single model-dataset pair (Qwen-continuation) and lack bootstrap confidence intervals; cross-model validation on Pythia and OLMo is pending.

The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$, with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.

\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:discuss_transfer}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs.
At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across generators.

The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.

Two caveats bound this conclusion.
First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:discuss_features}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.

This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.

The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}

Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11).
Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).

This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.

\emph{Model scale.}
All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.

\emph{Language and domain.}
All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
Sensitivity analysis across four decoding configurations shows $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 2$ for $\theta \in [0.60, 0.65]$, and $\Kempirical = 1$ at $\theta = 0.70$ (3 of 4 configurations).
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary---as the neural probe results confirm, where a richer representation pushes the 2v3 pair above $\theta$ on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}).
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
Preliminary neural probing results provide direct evidence for this gap: on the Qwen-continuation dataset, a frozen-encoder MLP achieves $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.6195$) compared to $\Kempirical = 2$ with 15-dimensional hand-crafted features (2v3 $\auc = 0.5609$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
This confirms that the 15D feature set does not saturate the available depth signal and that $\Ktheory \geq 3$.
However, the neural probe result rests on a single dataset and awaits cross-model validation and bootstrap confidence intervals before a firm revision of the headline $\Kempirical$ can be claimed.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is not optimal.
A preliminary neural probing experiment demonstrates that frozen LLM embeddings (1536 dimensions) paired with a lightweight MLP push $\Kempirical$ from~2 to~3 on the Qwen-continuation dataset (Section~\ref{sec:discuss_kstar}), confirming that learned representations capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss.
The magnitude of the gain---2v3 $\auc$ rising from 0.5609 to 0.6195---indicates meaningful recoverable signal beyond what hand-crafted features extract.
Full characterization of this gap, including cross-model generalization and bootstrap uncertainty quantification, remains future work.

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal regression methods exploit the natural ordering among class labels to improve generalization over nominal classifiers.
Cao et al.~\cite{cao2020coral} introduced CORAL, which enforces rank consistency through weight sharing in the output layer, guaranteeing that predicted cumulative probabilities are monotonically non-increasing.
Ordinal approaches have been applied in NLP tasks such as sentiment intensity prediction and essay scoring, where adjacent categories share more semantic overlap than distant ones.
Generational depth exhibits the same ordinal structure: text at depth~$k$ is distributionally closer to depth~$k\!\pm\!1$ than to depth~$k\!\pm\!3$, because each recursive generation step introduces an incremental distributional shift rather than a discontinuous one.
Despite this natural fit, ordinal classification has not been applied to synthetic text depth estimation.
The idea of decomposing ordinal problems into a series of binary decisions dates to Frank \& Hall~\cite{frank2001ordinal}; our Ordinal Boundary Detection (OBD) head follows this principle by learning $K\!-\!1$ cumulative boundary classifiers, yielding monotonic depth predictions and stronger calibration than a flat softmax baseline.

\paragraph{Probing Classifiers.}
Linear and shallow MLP probes have become a standard tool for analyzing what information is encoded in pretrained representations~\cite{alain2017understanding,conneau2018probing}.
Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022probing} surveys the methodology and cautions that probe complexity must be controlled to ensure that performance reflects representational content rather than probe capacity.
Our neural probe experiment follows this protocol: a two-layer MLP on frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings, where the probe's limited capacity ensures that discriminability reflects depth information already present in the representations rather than learned de novo.
